macadamize.etymology: From John Loudon McAdam, who introduced the process into Great Britain in 1816.

macaroon.etymology: F. macaron, It. maccherone. See Macaroni.

macaw.etymology: From the native name in the Antilles.

mace.etymology: Jav. & Malay. mas, fr. Skr. masha a bean.

macedoine.etymology: F., apparently the same word as Macédoine Macedonia.

machicolation.etymology: Cf. LL. machicolamentum, machacolladura, F. mâchicolis, mâchecoulis; perh. fr. F. mèche match, combustible matter + OF. coulis, couleis, flowing, fr. OF. & F. couler to flow. Cf. Match for making fire, and Cullis.

machinate.etymology: L. machinatus, p. p. of machinari to devise, plot. See Machine.

machine.etymology: F., fr. L. machina machine, engine, device, trick, Gr. Mechanic.

mackerel.etymology: OF. maquerel, F. maquereau, fr. D. makelaar mediator, agent, fr. makelen to act as agent.

mackinaw.etymology: From Mackinac,the State of Michigan, where blankets and other stores were distributed to the Indians.

roots.meaning: A combining form signifying long, large, great; as macrodiagonal, macrospore.
A combining form signifying long, large, great; as macrodiagonal, macrospore.

macula.etymology: L., spot, stain, blot. See Mail armor, and cf. Mackle, Macule.

maculate.etymology: L. maculatus, p. p. of maculare to spot. See Macula, and cf. Macule, v.

mad.etymology: AS. ma; akin to D. & G. made, Goth. mapa, and prob. to E. moth.

madame.etymology: F., fr. ma my (L. mea) + dame dame. See Dame, and cf. Madonna.

madder.etymology: OE. mader, AS. mædere; akin to Icel. ma.

madeira.etymology: Pg., the Island Madeira, properly, wood, fr. L. materia stuff, wood. The island was so called because well wooded. See Matter.

mademoiselle.etymology: F., fr. ma my, f. of mon + demoiselle young lady. See Damsel.

madia.etymology: NL., fr. Sp. madi, fr. Chilian madi, the native name.

madonna.etymology: It. madonna my lady. See Dame, Donna, and cf. Madame, Monkey.

madrigal.etymology: It. madrigale, OIt. madriale, mandriale (cf. LL. matriale); of uncertain origin, possibly fr. It mandra flock, L. mandra stall, herd of cattle, Gr. madrigal, originally, a pastoral song.

maestro.etymology: It., fr. L. magister. See Master.

magazine.etymology: F. magasin, It. magazzino, or Sp. magacen, almagacen; all fr. Ar. makhzan, almakhzan, a storehouse, granary, or cellar.

magdalen.etymology: From Mary Magdalene, traditionally reported to have been the repentant sinner forgiven by Christ. See Luke vii. 36.

maggot.etymology: W. macai, pl. maceiod, magiod, a worn or grub; cf. magu to bread.

magi.etymology: L., pl. of Magus, Gr. Mage, Magic.

magic.etymology: OE. magique, L. magice, Gr. Magic, a., and Magi.

magical.etymology: L. magicus, Gr. magique. See Magi.

magistrate.etymology: L. magistratus, fr. magister master: cf. F. magistrat. See Master.

magnanimous.etymology: L. magnanimus; magnus great + animus mind. See Magnate, and Animus.

magnate.etymology: F. magnat, L. (pl.) magnates, magnati, fr. magnus great. See Master.

magnesia.etymology: L. Magnesia, fem. of Magnesius of the country Magnesia, Gr. Magnet.

magnet.etymology: OE. magnete, OF. magnete, L. magnes, -etis, Gr. Magnesia, Manganese.

roots.meaning: A prefix meaning pertaining to, produced by, or in some way connected with, magnetism.
A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.

A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

magnificence.etymology: F. magnificence, L. magnificentia. See Magnific.

magnify.etymology: OE. magnifien, F. magnifier, L. magnificare. See Magnific.

magniloquent.etymology: L. magnus great + loquens, -entis, p. pr. of loqui to speak. See Magnitude, Loquacious.

magnitude.etymology: L. magnitudo, from magnus great. See Master, and cf. Maxim.

magnolia.etymology: NL. Named after Pierre Magnol, professor of botany at Montpellier, France, in the 17th century.

magnum.etymology: Neut. sing. of L. magnus great.

magpie.etymology: OE. & Prov. E. magot pie, maggoty pie, fr. Mag, Maggot, equiv. to Margaret, and fr. F. Marquerite, and common name of the magpie. Marguerite is fr. L. margarita pearl, Gr. Pie magpie, and cf. the analogous names Tomtit, and Jackdaw.

maguey.etymology: Sp. maguey, Mexican maguei and metl.

maharajah.etymology: Skr. maharaja; mahat great + raja king.

mahout.etymology: Hind. mahawat, Skr. mahamatra; mahat great + matra measure.

mahratta.etymology: Hind. Marhata, Marhatta, the name of a famous Hindoo race, from the old Skr. name Maha-rashtra.

maiden.etymology: OE. maiden, meiden, AS. mægden, dim. of AS. mæg, fr. mago son, servant; akin to G. magd, mädchen, maid, OHG. magad, Icel. mögr son, Goth. magus boy, child, magaps virgin, and perh. to Zend. magu youth. Cf. Maid a virgin.

roots.meaning: A termination denoting state, condition, quality, character, totality, as in manhood, childhood, knighthood, brotherhood. Sometimes it is written, chiefly in obsolete words, in the form - head.

mail.etymology: F. maille, OF. also maaille, LL. medalia. See Medal.

mailing.etymology: Scot., fr. mail tribute, rent. See 2d Mail.

maim.etymology: OE. maimen, OF. mahaignier, mehaignier, meshaignier, cf. It. magagnare, LL. mahemiare, mahennare; perh. of Celtic origin; cf. Armor. mac'ha to mutilate, mac'ha to crowd, press; or cf. OHG. mang to lack, perh. akin to E. mangle to lacerate. Cf. Mayhem.

main.etymology: F. main hand, L. manus. See Manual.

mainly.etymology: From main strong. See Main strength.

maintain.etymology: OE. maintenen, F. maintenir, properly, to hold by the hand; main hand (L. manus) + F. tenir to hold (L.tenere). See Manual, and Tenable.

maintenance.etymology: From Middle English mayntenaunce , from Old French maintenance , from maintenir , from Latin manus tenēre ( “ to hold in the hand ” ) . By surface analysis , maintain +‎ -ance .

majesty.etymology: OE. magestee, F. majesté, L. majestas, fr. an old compar. of magnus great. See Major, Master.

major.etymology: L. major, compar. of magnus great: cf. F. majeur. Cf. Master, Mayor, Magnitude, More, a.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.
. A prefix in composition denoting ill,or evil, F. male, adv., fr. malus, bad, ill. In some words it has the form male-, as in malediction, malevolent. See Malice.

malady.etymology: F. maladie, fr. malade ill, sick, OF. also, malabde, fr. L. male habitus, i. e., ill-kept, not in good condition. See Malice, and Habit.

malaise.etymology: F., fr. mal ill + aise ease.

malapropism.etymology: From Mrs. Malaprop, a character in Sheridan's drama, " The Rivals," who makes amusing blunders in her use of words. See Malapropos.

malapropos.etymology: F. mal à propos; mal evil + à propos to the purpose.

malar.etymology: L. mala the cheek: cf. F. malaire.

malaria.etymology: It., contr. fr. malaaria bad air. See Malice, and Air.

malcontent.etymology: F., fr. mal ill + content. See Malice, Content.

maledict.etymology: L. maledictus, p. p. of maledicere.

malediction.etymology: L. maledictio: cf. F. malédiction. See Maledicent.

malefactor.etymology: L., fr. malefacere to do evil; male ill, evil + facere to do. See Malice, and Fact.

malefic.etymology: L. maleficus: cf. F. maléfique. See Malefaction.

malevolent.etymology: L. malevolens, -entis; male ill + volens, p. pr. of velle to be willing or disposed, to wish. See Malice, and Voluntary.

malfeasance.etymology: F. malfaisance, fr. malfaisant injurious, doing ill; mal ill, evil + faisant doing, p. pr. of faire to do. See Malice, Feasible, and cf. Maleficence.

roots.meaning: . A prefix in composition denoting ill,or evil, F. male, adv., fr. malus, bad, ill. In some words it has the form male-, as in malediction, malevolent. See Malice.

malice.etymology: F. malice, fr. L. malitia, from malus bad, ill, evil, prob. orig., dirty, black; cf. Gr. mala dirt. Cf. Mauger.

malicious.etymology: Of. malicius, F. malicieux, fr. L. malitiosus. See Malice.

malign.etymology: L. malignus, for maligenus, i. e., of a bad kind or nature; malus bad + the root of genus birth, race, kind: cf. F. malin, masc., maligne, fem. See Malice, Gender, and cf. Benign, Malignant.

malignant.etymology: L. malignans, -antis, p. pr. of malignare, malignari, to do or make maliciously. See Malign, and cf. Benignant.

malingerer.etymology: F. malingre sickly, weakly, prob. from mal ill + OF. heingre, haingre, thin, lean, infirm, fr. L. aeger.

mall.etymology: OE. malle, F. mail, L. malleus. Cf. Malleus.

mallard.etymology: F. malari,fr. mâle male + -art =-ard. See Male, a., and -ard.

roots.meaning: The termination of many English words; as, coward, reynard, drunkard, mostly from the French, in which language this ending is of German origin, being orig. the same word as English hard. It usually has the sense of one who has to a high or excessive degree the quality expressed by the root; as, braggart, sluggard.

malleable.etymology: F. malléable, fr. LL. malleare to hammer. See Malleate.

mallet.etymology: F. maillet, dim. of mail. See Mall a beetle.

malleus.etymology: L., hammer. See Mall a beetle.

mallow.etymology: OE. malwe, AS. mealwe, fr. L. malva, akin to Gr. mala`chh; cf. mala`ssein to soften, malako`s soft. Named either from its softening or relaxing properties, or from its soft downy leaves. Cf. Mauve, Malachite.

malmsey.etymology: OE. malvesie, F. malvoisie, It. malvasia, malavagia, fr. Malvasia, or Napoli di Malvasia, in the Morea.

malt.etymology: AS. mealt; akin to D. mout, G. malz, Icel., Sw., & Dan. malt, and E. melt. sq. root108. See Melt.

malversation.etymology: F., fr. malverser to be corrupt in office, fr. L. male ill + versari to move about, to occupy one's self, vertere to turn. See Malice, and Verse.

mamma.etymology: Reduplicated from the infantine word ma, influenced in spelling by L. mamma.

mammal.etymology: L. mammalis belonging to the breast, fr. mamma the breast or pap: cf. F. mammal.

mammalia.etymology: NL., from L. mammalis. See Mammal.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

mammilla.etymology: L., dim. of mamma a breast.

mammon.etymology: L. mammona, Gr. mam; cf. Heb. matm a hiding place, subterranean storehouse, treasury, fr. taman to hide.

mammoth.etymology: Russ. mâmont, mámant, fr. Tartar mamma the earth. Certain Tartar races, the Tungooses and Yakoots, believed that the mammoth worked its way in the earth like a mole.

man.etymology: AS. mann, man, monn, mon; akin to OS., D., & OHG. man, G. mann, Icel. maedhr, for mannr, Dan. Mand, Sw. man, Goth. manna, Skr. manu, manus, and perh. to Skr. man to think, and E. mind. sq. root104. Cf. Minx a pert girl.

manacle.etymology: OE. manicle, OF. manicle, F. manicle sort glove, manacle, L. manicula a little hand, dim. of manus hand; cf. L. manica sleeve, manacle, fr.manus. See Manual.

manage.etymology: F. manège, It. maneggio, fr. maneggiare to manage, fr. L.manushand. Perhaps somewhat influenced by F. ménage housekeeping, OF. mesnage, akin to E. mansion. See Manual, and cf. Manege.

manakin.etymology: Cf. F. & G. manakin; prob. the native name.

manatee.etymology: Sp. manatí, from the native name in Hayti. Cf. Lamantin.

mandamus.etymology: L., we command, fr. mandare to command.

mandarin.etymology: Pg. mandarim, from Malay mantri minister of state, prop. a Hind. word, fr. Skr. mantrin a counselor, manira a counsel, man to think.

mandatary.etymology: L. mandatarius, fr. mandatum a charge, commission, order: cf. F. mandataire. See Mandate.

mandate.etymology: L. mandatum, fr. mandare to commit to one's charge, order, orig., to put into one's hand; manus hand + dare to give: cf. F. mandat. See Manual, Date a time, and cf. Commend, Maundy Thursday.

mandible.etymology: L. mandibula, mandibulum, fr. mandere to chew. Cf. Manger.

mandolin.etymology: F. mandoline, It. mandolino, dim. of mandola, fr. L. pandura. See Bandore.

mandrake.etymology: AS. mandragora, L. mandragoras, fr. Gr. mandragore.

mandrel.etymology: F. mandrin, prob. through (assumed) LL. mamphurinum, fr. L. mamphur a bow drill.

mandrill.etymology: Cf. F. mandrille, Sp. mandril, It. mandrillo; prob. the native name in Africa. Cf. Drill an ape.

manducate.etymology: L. manducatus, p. p. of manducare to chew. See Manger.

mane.etymology: AS. manu; akin to OD. mane, D. maan, G. mähne, OHG. mana, Icel. mön, Dan. & Sw. man, AS. mene necklace, Icel. men, L. monile, Gr. manya neck muscles. sq. root275.

maneuver.etymology: F. manoeuvre, OF. manuevre, LL. manopera, lit., hand work, manual labor; L.manus hand + opera, fr. opus work. See Manual, Operate, and cf. Mainor, Manure.

mangabey.etymology: So called by Buffon from Mangaby, in Madagascar, where he erroneously supposed them be native.

manganese.etymology: F. manganèse, It. mamaganese, sasso magnesio; prob. corrupted from L. magnes, because of its resemblance to the magnet. See Magnet, and cf. Magnesia.

manger.etymology: F. mangeoire, fr. manger to eat, fr. L. manducare, fr. mandere to chew. Cf. Mandible, Manducate.

mangle.etymology: A frequentative fr. OE. manken to main, AS. mancian, in bemancian to mutilate, fr. L. mancus maimed; perh. akin to G. mangeln to be wanting.

mangonel.etymology: OF. mangonel, LL. manganellus, manganum, fr. Gr. Mangle, n.

mangy.etymology: F. mangé, p. p. of manger to eat. See Manger.

roots.meaning: A termination denoting state, condition, quality, character, totality, as in manhood, childhood, knighthood, brotherhood. Sometimes it is written, chiefly in obsolete words, in the form - head.

mania.etymology: L. mania, Gr. manie, F. manie. Cf. Mind, n., Necromancy.

manicure.etymology: F., fr. L. manus hand + curare to cure.

manifest.etymology: F. manifeste, L. manifestus, lit., struck by the hand, hence, palpable; manus hand + fendere (in comp.) to strike. See Manual, and Defend.

manifesto.etymology: It. manifesto. See Manifest, n. & a.

manifold.etymology: AS. manigfeald. See Many, and Fold.

manikin.etymology: OD. manneken, dim. of man man. See Man, and - kin.

manilla.etymology: Sp. manilla; cf. It. maniglio, maniglia; F. manille; Pg. manilha; all fr. L. manus hand, and formed after the analogy of L. monile, pl. monilia, necklace: cf. F. manille.

manipulate.etymology: LL. manipulatus, p. p. of manipulare to lead by the hand, fr. L. manipulus. See Maniple.

manis.etymology: NL., fr. L. manes the ghosts or shades of the dead. So called from its dismal appearance, and because it seeks for its food by night.

mankind.etymology: AS. mancynn. See Kin kindred, Kind, n.

roots.meaning: A suffix forming adjectives and adverbs, and denoting likeness or resemblance.

manna.etymology: L., fr. Gr. man; cf. Ar. mann, properly, gift (of heaven).

manner.etymology: OE. manere, F. manière, from OF. manier, adj., manual, skillful, handy, fr. (assumed) LL. manarius, for L. manuarius belonging to the hand, fr. manus the hand. See Manual.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to from adjectives from nouns and from adjectives. It denotes relation, resemblance, similarity, and sometimes has a diminutive force; as, selfish, boyish, brutish; whitish, somewhat white.
A suffix denoting that the substance in the name of which it appears belongs to the series of alcohols or hydroxyl derivatives, as carbinol, glycerol, etc.

manoeuvre.etymology: F. manoeuvre, OF. manuevre, LL. manopera, lit., hand work, manual labor; L.manus hand + opera, fr. opus work. See Manual, Operate, and cf. Mainor, Manure.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

manor.etymology: OE. maner, OF. maneir habitation, village, F. manoir manor, prop. the OF. inf. maneir to stay, remain, dwell, L. manere, and so called because it was the permanent residence of the lord and of his tenants. See Mansion, and cf. Remain.

manse.etymology: LL. mansa, mansus, mansum, a farm, fr. L. manere, mansum, to stay, dwell. See Mansion, Manor.

mansion.etymology: OF. mansion, F. maison, fr. L. mansio a staying, remaining, a dwelling, habitation, fr. manere, mansum, to stay, dwell; akin to Gr. Manse, Manor, Menagerie, Menial, Permanent.

mantel.etymology: The same word as mantle a garment; cf. F. manteau de cheminée. See Mantle.

mantelet.etymology: F., dim. of manteau, OF. mantel. See Mantle.

mantissa.etymology: L., an addition, makeweight; of Tuscan origin.

mantle.etymology: OE. mantel, OF. mantel, F. manteau, fr. L. mantellum, mantelum, a cloth, napkin, cloak, mantle (cf. mantele, mantile, towel, napkin); prob. from manus hand + the root of tela cloth. See Manual, Textile, and cf. Mandil, Mantel, Mantilla.

manual.etymology: OE. manuel, F. manuel, L. manualis, fr. manus hand; prob. akin to AS. mund hand, protection, OHG. munt, G. mündel a ward, vormund guardian, Icel. mund hand. Cf. Emancipate, Legerdemain, Maintain, Manage, Manner, Manur, Mound a hill.

manufactory.etymology: Cf. L. factorium an oil press, prop., place where something is made. See Manufacture.

manufacture.etymology: L. manus the hand + factura a making, fr. facere to make: cf. F. manufacture. See Manual, and Fact.

manumission.etymology: L. manumissio: cf. F. manumission. See Manumit.

manumit.etymology: L. manumittere, manumissum; manus the hand + mittere to send, to send off. See Manual, and Missile.

manure.etymology: Contr, from OF. manuvrer, manovrer, to work with the hand, to cultivate by manual labor, F. man. See Manual, Ure, Opera, and cf. Inure.

manuscript.etymology: L. manu scriptus. See Manual, and Scribe.

manzanita.etymology: Sp., dim. of munzana an apple.

map.etymology: From F. mappe, in mappemonde map of the world, fr. L. mappa napkin, signal cloth; -- a Punic word. Cf. Apron, Napkin, Nappe.

maple.etymology: AS. mapolder, mapulder, mapol; akin to Icel. möpurr; cf. OHG. mazzaltra, mazzoltra, G. massholder.

mar.etymology: OE. marren, merren, AS. merran, myrran (in comp.), to obstruct, impede, dissipate; akin to OS. merrian, OHG. marrjan, merran; cf. D. marren, meeren, to moor a ship, Icel. merja to bruise, crush, and Goth. marzjan to offend. Cf. Moor, v.

marabout.etymology: F., from Pg. marabuto, Ar. morabit. Cf. Maravedi.

maraschino.etymology: It., fr. marasca, amarasca, a sour cherry, L. amarus bitter.

maraud.etymology: F. marauder, fr. maraud vagabond, OF. marault; of uncertain origin, perh. for malault, fr. (assumed) LL. malaldus; fr. L. malus bad, ill + a suffix of German origin (cf. Herald). Cf. Malice.

marauder.etymology: From Maraud, v.: cf. F. maraudeur.

marble.etymology: OE. marbel, marbre, F. marbre, L. marmor, fr. Gr. Marmoreal.

march.etymology: L. Martius mensis Mars'month fr. Martius belonging to Mars, the god of war: cf. F. mars. Cf. Martial.

marchioness.etymology: LL. marchionissa, fr. marchio a marquis. See Marquis.

marchpane.etymology: Cf. It. marzapane,Sp. pan,. massepain, prob. fr. L. maza frumenty (Gr. ma^za) + L. panis bread; but perh. the first part of the word is from the name of the inventor.

mare.etymology: OE. mere, AS. mere, myre, fem of AS. mearh horse, akin to D. merrie mare, G. mähre, OHG. marah horse, meriha mare, Icel. marr horse, OCelt. marka (Pausan. 19, 19,4), Ir. marc, W. march. Cf. Marshal.

margin.etymology: OE. margine, margent, L. margo, ginis. Cf. March a border, Marge.

margrave.etymology: G. markgraf, prop., lord chief justice of the march; mark bound, border, march + graf earl, count, lord chief justice; cf. Goth. gagrëfts decree: cf. D. markgraaf, F. margrave. See March border, and cf. Landgrave, Graff.

marguerite.etymology: F., a pearl, a daisy. See Margarite.

marinade.etymology: F.: cf. It. marinato marinade, F. mariner to preserve food for use at sea. See Marinate.

marine.etymology: L. marinus, fr. mare the sea: cf. F. marin. See Mere a pool.

mariner.etymology: F. marinier, LL. marinarius. See Marine.

marionette.etymology: F. marionette, prop. a dim. of Marie Mary.

marital.etymology: F., fr. L. maritalis, fr. maritus belonging to marriage, n., a husband. See Marry, v.

maritime.etymology: L. maritimus, fr. mare the sea: cf. F. maritime. See Mere a pool.

market.etymology: Akin to D. markt, OHG. markat, merkat, G. markt; all fr.L. mercatus trade, market place, fr. mercari, p. p. mercatus, to trade, traffic, merx, mercis, ware, merchandise, prob. akin to merere to deserve, gain, acquire: cf. F. marché. See Merit, and cf. Merchant, Mart.

marline.etymology: LG. marlien, marling, or D. marling, marlijn, fr. D. marren to tie, prob. akin to E. moor, v., and lijn line: cf.F. merlin. See Moor, v., Line.

marlite.etymology: Cf. F. marlite. See Marl, n.

marmalade.etymology: F. marmelade, Pg. marmelada, fr. marmélo a quince, fr. L. melimelum honey apple, Gr. Mellifluous, Melon.

marmoreal.etymology: L. marmoreus, fr. marmor marble: cf. F. marmoréen. See Marble.

marmorean.etymology: L. marmoreus, fr. marmor marble: cf. F. marmoréen. See Marble.

marmoset.etymology: F. marmouset a grotesque figure, an ugly little boy, prob. fr. LL. marmoretum, fr. L. marmor marble. Perhaps confused with marmot. See Marble.

marmot.etymology: It. marmotta, marmotto, prob. fr. L. mus montanus, or mus montis, lit., mountain mouse or rat. See Mountain, and Mouse.

maroon.etymology: F. marron, abbrev. fr. Sp. cimarron wild, unruly, from cima the summit of a mountain; hence, negro cimarron a runaway negro that lives in the mountains.

marque.etymology: F. marque, in lettre de marque letter of marque, a commission with which the commandant of every armed vessel was obliged to be provided, under penalty of being considered a pirate or corsair; marque here prob. meaning, border, boundary (the letter of marque being a permission to go beyond the border), and of German origin. See March border.

marquee.etymology: F. marquise, misunderstood as a plural; prob. orig., tent of the marchioness. See Marquis.

marquetry.etymology: F. marqueterie, from marqueter to checker, inlay, fr. marque mark, sign; of German origin. See Mark a sign.

marquis.etymology: F. marquis, OF. markis, marchis, LL. marchensis; of German origin; cf. G. mark bound, border, march, OHG. marcha. See March border, and cf. Marchioness, Marquee, Marquess.

marquise.etymology: F. See Marquis, and cf. Marquee.

marriage.etymology: OE. mariage, F. mariage. See Marry, v. t.

marrow.etymology: OE. marou, mary, maruh, AS. mearg, mearh; akin to OS. marg, D. merg, G. Mark, OHG. marg, marag, Icel. mergr, Sw. merg, Dan. marv, Skr. majjan; cf. Skr. majj to sink, L. mergere. sq. root274 Cf. Merge.

marry.etymology: OE. marien, F. marier, L. maritare, fr. maritus husband, fr. mas, maris, a male. See Male, and cf. Maritral.

mars.etymology: L. Mars, gen. Martis, archaic Mavors, gen. Mavortis.

marsh.etymology: OE. mersch, AS. mersc, fr. mere lake. See Mere pool, and cf. Marish, Morass.

marshal.etymology: OE. mareschal, OF. mareschal, F. maréchal, LL. mariscalcus, from OHG. marah-scalc (G. marschall); marah horse + scalc servant (akin to AS. scealc, Goth. skalks). F. maréchal signifies, a marshal, and a farrier. See Mare horse, and cf. Seneschal.

martagon.etymology: Cf. F. & Sp. martagon, It. martagone.

marten.etymology: From older martern, marter, martre, F. martre, marte, LL. martures (pl.), fr. L. martes; akin to AS. mear, meard, G. marder, OHG. mardar, Icel. mör. Cf. Foumart.

martial.etymology: F., fr. L. martialis of or belonging to Mars, the god of war. Cf. March the month.

martinet.etymology: So called from an officer of that name in the French army under Louis XIV. Cf. Martin the bird, Martlet.

martingale.etymology: F. martingale; cf. It. martingala a sort of hose, martingale, Sp. martingala a greave, cuish, martingale, Sp. almártaga a kind of bridle.

martyr.etymology: AS., from L. martyr, Gr. ma`rtyr, ma`rtys, prop., a witness; cf. Skr. smrs to remember, E. memory.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting: (a) Jurisdiction or property and jurisdiction, dominion, as in kingdom earldom. (b) State, condition, or quality of being, as in wisdom, freedom.

marvel.etymology: OE. mervaile, F. merveille, fr. L. mirabilia wonderful things, pl., fr. mirabilis wonderful, fr. mirari to wonder or marvel at. See Admire, Smile, and cf. Miracle.

marvelous.etymology: OE. merveillous, OF. merveillos, F. Merveilleux. See Marvel, n.

mascot.etymology: Through French fr. Pr. mascot a little sorcerer or magician, mascotto witchcraft, sorcery.

masculine.etymology: L. masculinus, fr. masculus male, manly, dim. of mas a male: cf. F. masculin. See Male masculine.

mash.etymology: Akin to G. meisch, maisch, meische, maische, mash, wash, and prob. to AS. miscian to mix. See Mix.

mask.etymology: F. masque, LL. masca, mascha, mascus; cf. Sp. & Pg. máscara, It. maschera; all fr. Ar. maskharat buffoon, fool, pleasantry, anything ridiculous or mirthful, fr. sakhira to ridicule, to laugh at. Cf. Masque, Masquerade.

mason.etymology: F. ma, LL. macio, machio, mattio, mactio, marcio, macerio; of uncertain origin.

masquerade.etymology: F. mascarade, fr. Sp. mascarada, or It. mascherata. See Mask.

mass.etymology: OE. masse, messe, AS. mæsse. LL. missa, from L. mittere, missum, to send, dismiss: cf. F. messe. In the ancient churches, the public services at which the catechumens were permitted to be present were called missa catechumenorum, ending with the reading of the Gospel. Then they were dismissed with these words : "Ite, missa est" [sc. ecclesia], the congregation is dismissed. After that the sacrifice proper began. At its close the same words were said to those who remained. So the word gave the name of Mass to the sacrifice in the Catholic Church. See Missile, and cf. Christmas, Lammas, Mess a dish, Missal.

massacre.etymology: F., fr. LL. mazacrium; cf. Prov. G. metzgern, metzgen, to kill cattle, G. metzger a butcher, and LG. matsken to cut, hew, OHG. meizan to cut, Goth. máitan.

masseur.etymology: F., or formed in imitation of French. See Massage.

masseuse.etymology: F., or formed in imitation of French. See Massage.

massicot.etymology: F. massicot; E. masticot is a corruption.

mast.etymology: AS. mæst, fem. ; akin to G. mast, and E. meat. See Meat.

master.etymology: OE. maistre, maister, OF. maistre, mestre, F. maître, fr. L. magister, orig. a double comparative from the root of magnus great, akin to Gr. Maestro, Magister, Magistrate, Magnitude, Major, Mister, Mistress, Mickle.

mastic.etymology: F., fr. L. mastiche, mastichum, Gr. [Written also mastich.

masticate.etymology: L. masticatus, p. p. of masticare to chew, prob. fr. mastiche mastic. See Mastic.

mastiff.etymology: Prob. fr. Prov. E. masty, adj., large, n., a great dog, prob. fr. mast fruit, and hence, lit., fattened with mast. There is perh. confusion with OF. mestif mongrel; cf. also F. mâtin mastiff, OF. mastin.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

masturbation.etymology: L. masturbatus, p. p. of masturbari to practice onanism: cf. F. masturbation.

matador.etymology: Sp. matador, prop., a killer, fr. matar to kill, L. mactare to sacrifice, kill.

match.etymology: OE. macche, F. mèche, F. mèche, fr. L. myxa a lamp nozzle, Gr. Mucus.

matelote.etymology: F., fr. matelot a sailor; properly, a dish such as sailors prepare.

material.etymology: L. materialis, fr. materia stuff, matter: cf. F. matériel. See Matter, and cf. MatÉriel.

maternal.etymology: F. maternel, L. maternus, fr. mater mother. See Mother.

math.etymology: AS. mmawan to mow, G. mahd math. See Mow to cut (grass).

mathematics.etymology: F. mathématiques, pl., L. mathematica, sing., Gr. Mathematic, and -ics.

roots.meaning: . A suffix used in forming the names of certain sciences, systems, etc., as acoustics, mathematics, dynamics, statistics, politics, athletics.
A suffix meaning a ruler, as in monarch (a sole ruler).

matricide.etymology: L. matricidium; mater mother + coedere to kill, slay: cf. F. matricide. See Mother, and cf. Homicide.

matriculate.etymology: L. matricula a public roll or register, dim. of matrix a mother, in respect to propagation, also, a public register. See Matrix.

matrimonial.etymology: L. matrimonialis: cf. F. matrimonial. See Matrimony.

matrimony.etymology: OE. matrimoine, through Old French, fr. L. matrimonium, fr. mater mother. See Mother.

matrix.etymology: L., fr. mater mother. See Mother, and cf. Matrice.

matron.etymology: F. matrone, L. matrona, fr. mater mother. See Mother.

matronymic.etymology: L. mater mother + -nymic, as in patronimic.

matte.etymology: F. matte; cf. F. mat, masc., matte, fem., faint, dull, dim; -- said of metals. See Mate checkmate.

matter.etymology: OE. matere, F. matière, fr. L. materia; perh. akin to L. mater mother. Cf. Mother, Madeira, Material.

mattress.etymology: OF. materas, F. matelas, LL. matratium; cf. Sp. & Pg. almadraque, Pr. almatrac; all from Ar. matsrah a place where anything is thrown, what is thrown under something, fr. tsaraha to throw.

maturate.etymology: L. maturatus, p. p. of maturare to make ripe, fr. maturus ripe, mature. See Mature, v. & a.

maturation.etymology: L. maturatio a hastening: cf. F. maturation.

mature.etymology: L. maturus; prob. akin to E. matin.

matutinal.etymology: L. matutinalis, matutinus: cf. F. matutinal. See Matin.

maudlin.etymology: From Maudlin, a contr. of Magdalen, OE. Maudeleyne, who is drawn by painters with eyes swelled and red with weeping.

maunder.etymology: Cf. F. mendier to beg, E. mendicant.

mauve.etymology: F., mallow, L. malva. So named from the similarity of the color to that of the petals of common mallow, Malva sylvestris. See Mallow.

mavis.etymology: F. mauvis, Arm. milvid, milfid, milc'hhouid, Corn. melhuez.

maxilla.etymology: L., dim. of mala jaw, jawbone.

maxillary.etymology: L. maxillaris, fr. maxilla jawbone, jaw: cf. F. maxillaire.

maxim.etymology: F. maxime, L. maxima (sc. sententia), the greatest sentence, proposition, or axiom, i. e., of the greatest weight or authority, fem. fr. maximus greatest, superl. of magnus great. See Magnitude, and cf. Maximum.

maximum.etymology: L., neut. from maximus the greatest. See Maxim.

may.etymology: AS. pres. mæg I am able, pret. meahte, mihte; akin to D. mogen, G. mögen, OHG. mugan, magan, Icel. mega, Goth. magan, Russ. moche. Dismay, Main strength, Might. The old imp. mought is obsolete, except as a provincial word.

mayhem.etymology: The same as maim. See Maim.

mayor.etymology: OE. maire, F. maire, fr. L. major greater, higher, nobler, compar. of magnus great; cf. Sp. mayor. See Major, and cf. Merino.

mayoral.etymology: Sp., fr. mayor greater, L. major.

maze.etymology: OE. mase; cf. OE. masen to confuse, puzzle, Norweg. masast to fall into a slumber, masa to be continually busy, prate, chatter, Icel. masa to chatter, dial. Sw. masa to bask, be slow, work slowly and lazily, mas slow, lazy.

mazer.etymology: OE. maser, akin to OD. maser an excrescence on a maple tree, OHG. masar, G. maser spot, Icel. mösurr maple.

mead.etymology: OE. mede, AS. meodo; akin to D. mede, G. met, meth, OHG. metu, mitu, Icel. mjö, Dan. miöd, Sw. mjöd, Russ. med', Lith. midus, W. medd, Gr. madhu honey, a sweet drink, as adj., sweet. Metheglin.

meadow.etymology: AS. meady; akin to m, and to G. matte; prob. also to E. mow. See Mow to cut (grass), and cf. 2d Mead.

meager.etymology: OE. merge, F. maigre, L. macer; akin to D. & G. mager, Icel. magr, and prob. to Gr. Emaciate, Maigre.

meagre.etymology: OE. merge, F. maigre, L. macer; akin to D. & G. mager, Icel. magr, and prob. to Gr. Emaciate, Maigre.

meal.etymology: OE. mele, AS. m part, portion, portion of time; akin to E. meal a repast. Cf. Piecemeal.

mean.etymology: OE. menen, AS. mænan to recite, tell, intend, wish; akin to OS. menian to have in mind, mean, D. meenen, G. meinen, OHG. meinan, Icel. meina, Sw. mena, Dan. mene, and to E. mind. Mind, and cf. Moan.

meander.etymology: L. Maeander, orig., a river in Phrygia, proverbial for its many windings, Gr. méandre.

measurable.etymology: F. mesurable, L. mensurabilis. See Measure, and cf. Mensurable.

measure.etymology: OE. mesure, F. mesure, L. mensura, fr. metiri, mensus, to measure; akin to metrum poetical measure, Gr. meter. Cf. Immense, Mensuration, Mete to measure.

meat.etymology: OE. mete, AS. mete; akin to OS. mat, meti, D. met hashed meat, G. mettwurst sausage, OHG. maz food, Icel. matr, Sw. mat, Dan. mad, Goth. mats. Cf. Mast fruit, Mush.

meatus.etymology: L., a going, passage, fr. meare to go.

mechanic.etymology: F. mécanique mechanics. See Mechanic, a.

mechanism.etymology: Cf. F. mécanisme, L. mechanisma. See Mechanic.

medal.etymology: F. médaille, It. medaglia, fr. L. metallum metal, through (assumed) LL. metalleus made of metal. See Metal, and cf. Mail a piece of money.

medallion.etymology: F. médaillion, It. medaglione, augm. of medaglia. See Medal.

meddle.etymology: OE. medlen to mix, OF. medler, mesler, F. mêler, LL. misculare, a dim. fr. L. miscere to mix. Mix, and cf. Medley, Mellay.

mediaeval.etymology: L. medius middle + aevum age. See Middle, and Age.

medial.etymology: L. medialis, fr. medius middle: cf. F. médial. See Middle.

median.etymology: L. medianus, fr. medius middle. See Medial.

mediant.etymology: L. medians, p. p. of mediare to halve: cf. It. mediante, F. médiante.

mediastinum.etymology: NL. mediastinum, fr. L. medius middle; cf. mediastinus helper, a menial servant, LL. mediastinus equiv. to medius: cf F. médiastin.

mediate.etymology: L. mediatus, p. p. of mediare, v. t., to halve, v. i., to be in the middle. See Mid, and cf. Moiety.

mediation.etymology: OE. mediacioun, F. médiation. See Mediate, a.

mediatrix.etymology: L. mediatrix, f. of mediator: cf. F. médiatrice.

medical.etymology: LL. medicalis, L. medicus belonging to healing, fr. mederi to heal; cf. Zend madha medical science, wisdom, gr. mind: cf. F. médical.

medicament.etymology: L. medicamentum, fr. medicare, medicari, to heal: cf. F. médicament. See Medicable.

medicate.etymology: L. medicatus, p. p. of medicare, medicari. See Medicable.

medicinal.etymology: L. medicinalis: cf. F. médicinal. See Medicine.

medicine.etymology: L. medicina (sc. ars), fr. medicinus medical, fr. medicus: cf. F. médecine. See Medical.

mediocre.etymology: F. médiocre, L. mediocris, fr. medius middle. See Mid.

meditate.etymology: L. meditatus, p. p. of meditari to meditate; cf. Gr. mind.

meditation.etymology: OE. meditacioun, F. méditation, fr. L. meditatio.

mediterranean.etymology: L. mediterraneus; medius middle + terra land. See Mid, and Terrace.

medium.etymology: L. medium the middle, fr. medius middle. See Mid, and cf. Medius.

medlar.etymology: OE. medler medlar tree, OF. meslier, F. néflier, L. mespilum, mespilus, Gr. Naseberry.

medley.etymology: OE. medlee, OF. meslée, medlée, mellée, F. mêlée. See Meddle, and cf. MelÉe, Mellay.

medullary.etymology: L. medullaris, fr. medulla marrow: cf. F. médullaire.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

meed.etymology: OE. mede, AS. med, meord; akin to OS. m, OHG. miata, mieta, G. miethe hire, Goth. mizdo reward, Bohem. & Russ. mzda, Gr. mistho`s, Skr. midha. sq. root276.

meerschaum.etymology: G., lit., sea foam; meer sea + schaum foam; but it perh. is a corruption of the Tartaric name myrsen. Cf. Mere a lake, and Scum.

meet.etymology: OE. meten, AS. m, fr. m, gem, a meeting; akin to OS. m to meet, Icel. mæta, Goth. gam. See Moot, v. t.

roots.meaning: Combining forms fr. Gr. li`qos a stone; -- used chiefly in naming minerals and rocks.
Combining forms signifying: (a) Great, extended, powerful; as, megascope, megacosm. (b) (Metric System, Elec., Mech., etc.)

megalopolis.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. megalo`polis; me`gas, mega`lh, great + po`lis city.

megathere.etymology: NL. megatherium, fr. Gr. me`gas great + thyri`on beast.

megatherium.etymology: NL. megatherium, fr. Gr. me`gas great + thyri`on beast.

megrim.etymology: OE. migrim, migrene, F. migraine, LL. hemigrania, L. hemicrania, hemicranium, Gr. Hemi- and Cranium, and cf. Hemicrania, Migraine.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying half.

melancholy.etymology: OE. melancolie, F. mélancolie, L. melancholia, fr. Gr. Malice, and 1st Gall.

melanesian.etymology: Gr. Melanesia was so called from the dark complexion of the natives.

melee.etymology: F., fr. mêler to mix. See Meddle, Mell, and cf. Mellay.

meliorate.etymology: L. melioratus, p. p. of meliorare to meliorate, fr. melior better; akin to Gr. Ameliorate.

melissa.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. me`lissa a bee, honey.

mellifluous.etymology: L. mellifluus; mel, mellis, honey (akin to Gr. milip) + fluere to flow. See Mildew, Fluent, and cf. Marmalade.

mellow.etymology: OE. melwe; cf. AS. mearu soft, D. murw, Prov. G. mollig soft, D. malsch, and E. meal flour.

melody.etymology: OE. melodie, F. mélodie, L. melodia, fr. Gr. Ode.

melon.etymology: F., fr. L. melo, for melopepo an apple-shaped melon, Gr. malum apple. Cf. Marmalade.

melt.etymology: AS. meltan; akin to Gr. malt, and prob. to E. smelt, v. Smelt, v., Malt, Milt the spleen.

membrane.etymology: F., fr. L. membrana the skin that covers the separate members of the body, fr. L. membrum. See Member.

memento.etymology: L., remember, be mindful, imper. of meminisse to remember. See Mention.

memoir.etymology: F. mémoire, m., memorandum, fr. mémoire, f., memory, L. memoria. See Memory.

memorabilia.etymology: L., fr. memorabilis memorable. See Memorable.

memorable.etymology: L. memorabilis, fr. memorare to bring to remembrance, fr. memor mindful, remembering. See Memory, and cf. Memorabilia.

memorandum.etymology: L., something to be remembered, neut. of memorandus, fut. pass. p. of memorare. See Memorable.

memorial.etymology: F. mémorial, L. memorialis, fr. memoria. See Memory.

memory.etymology: OE. memorie, OF. memoire, memorie, F. mémoire, L. memoria, fr. memor mindful; cf. mora delay. Cf. Demur, Martyr, Memoir, Remember.

men.etymology: OE. me, men. "Not the plural of man, but a weakened form of the word man itself." Skeat.

menace.etymology: F., fr. L. minaciae threats, menaces, fr. minax, - acis, projecting, threatening, minae projecting points or pinnacles, threats. Cf. Amenable, Demean, Imminent, Minatory.

menagerie.etymology: F. ménagerie, fr. ménager to keep house, ménage household. See Menial, Mansion.

mendacious.etymology: L. mendax, -acis, lying, cf. mentiri to lie.

mendicant.etymology: L. mendicans, -antis, p. pr. of mendicare to beg, fr. mendicus beggar, indigent.

mendicity.etymology: L. mendicitas: cf. F. mendicité. See Mendicant.

menhir.etymology: F. Armor. men stone + hir high.

menial.etymology: OE. meneal, fr. meine, maine, household, OF. maisniée, maisnie, LL. mansionaticum. See Mansion, and cf. Meine, n., Meiny.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

meniscus.etymology: NL., from Gr. mh`nh the moon.

menses.etymology: L. mensis month, pl. menses months, and the monthly courses of women. Cf. Month.

menstrual.etymology: L. menstrualis: cf. F. menstruel. See Menstruous.

mensurable.etymology: L. mensurabilis, fr. mensurare to measure, fr. mensura measure: cf. F. mensurable. See Measurable, Measure.

mensurate.etymology: L. mensuratus, p. p. of mensurare. See Measure, v.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that the substance in the name of which it appears belongs to the series of alcohols or hydroxyl derivatives, as carbinol, glycerol, etc.

mention.etymology: OE. mencioun, F. mention, L. mentio, from the root of meminisse to remember. See Mind.

mentor.etymology: From Mentor, the counselor of Telemachus, Gr. Monitor.

menu.etymology: F., slender, thin, minute. See 4th Minute.

mephitic.etymology: L. mephiticus, fr. mephitis mephitis: cf. F. méphitique.

mercantile.etymology: F. mercantile, It. mercantile, fr. L. mercans, -antis, p. pr. of mercari to traffic. See Merchant.

mercenary.etymology: OE. mercenarie, F. mercenaire, fr. L. mercenarius, fr. merces wages, reward. See Mercy.

mercer.etymology: F. mercier, fr. L. merx, mercis, wares, merchandise. See Merchant.

mercerize.etymology: From (John) Mercer (1791-1866), an English calico printer who introduced the process + -ize.

roots.meaning: A verb suffix signifying to make, to do, to practice; as apologize, baptize, theorize, tyrannize.

merchant.etymology: OE. marchant, OF. marcheant, F. marchand, fr. LL. mercatans, -antis, p. pr. of mercatare to negotiate, L. mercari to traffic, fr. merx, mercis, wares. See Market, Merit, and cf. Commerce.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying full of, abounding with; as, boastful, harmful, woeful.

mercurial.etymology: L. mercurialis, fr. Mercurius Mercury: cf. F. mercuriel.

mercury.etymology: L. Mercurius; akin to merx wares.

mercy.etymology: OE. merci, F. merci, L. merces, mercedis, hire, pay, reward, LL., equiv. to misericordia pity, mercy. L. merces is probmerere to deserve, acquire. See Merit, and cf. Amerce.

meretricious.etymology: L. meretricius, from meretrix, -icis, a prostitute, lit., one who earns money, i. e., by prostitution, fr. merere to earn, gain. See Merit.

merganser.etymology: Sp. mergánsar, fr. mergo a diver (L. mergus, fr. mergere to dip, dive) + ánsar goose, L. anser.

merge.etymology: L. mergere, mersum. Cf. Emerge, Immerse, Marrow.

meridian.etymology: F. méridien, L. meridianus pertaining to noon, fr. meridies noon, midday, for older medidies; medius mid, middle + dies day. See Mid, and Diurnal.

meridional.etymology: F. méridional, L. meridionalis, fr. meridies midday. See Meridian.

merino.etymology: Sp. merino moving from pasture to pasture, fr. merino a royal judge and superintendent or inspector of sheep walks, LL. merinus, fr. majorinus, i. e., major villmajor greater. See Major. Merino sheep are driven at certain seasons from one part of Spain to another, in large flocks, for pasturage.

merit.etymology: F. mérite, L. meritum, fr. merere, mereri, to deserve, merit; prob. originally, to get a share; akin to Gr. Market, Merchant, Mercer, Mercy.

meritorious.etymology: L. meritorius that brings in money.

merl.etymology: F. merle, L. merula, merulus. Cf. Ousel.

merle.etymology: F. merle, L. merula, merulus. Cf. Ousel.

merlin.etymology: OE. merlion, F. émerillon ; cf. OHG. smirl, G. schmerl ; prob. fr. L. merula blackbird. Cf. Merle.

merlon.etymology: F., perh. fr. L. moerus, for murus a wall, through (assumed) dim. moerulus.

mermaid.etymology: AS. mere lake, sea. See Mere lake, and maid.

merovingian.etymology: From Merovaeus, the Latin name of a king of the Franks.

merry.etymology: OE. merie, mirie, murie, merry, pleasant, AS. merge, myrige, pleasant; cf. murge, adv.; prob. akin to OHG. murg, short, Goth. gamaúrgjan to shorten; cf. L. murcus a coward, who cuts off his thumb to escape military service; the Anglo-Saxon and English meanings coming from the idea of making the time seem short. Cf. Mirth.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting in the middle, intermediate; specif. (Chem.), denoting a type of hydrocarbons which are regarded as methenyl derivatives. Also used adjectively.

mesh.etymology: AS. masc, max, m; akin to D. maas, masche, OHG. masca, Icel. möskvi; cf. Lith. mazgas a knot, megsti to weave nets, to knot.

mesmerism.etymology: From Mesmer, who first brought it into notice at Vienna, about 1775: cf. F. mesmérisme.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting in the middle, intermediate; specif. (Chem.), denoting a type of hydrocarbons which are regarded as methenyl derivatives. Also used adjectively.
A suffix or terminal formative, used principally in biological terms, and signifying growth, formation; as, bioblast, epiblast, mesoblast, etc.

mesquit.etymology: Sp. mezquite; said to be a Mexican Indian word.

mesquite.etymology: Sp. mezquite; said to be a Mexican Indian word.

mess.etymology: OE. mes, OF. mets, LL. missum, p. p. of mittere to put, place (e. g., on the table), L. mittere to send. See Mission, and cf. Mass religious service.

message.etymology: F., fr. LL. missaticum, fr. L. mittere, missum, to send. See Mission, and cf. Messenger.

messenger.etymology: OE. messager, OF. messagier, F. messager. See Message.

messiah.etymology: Heb. mashiakh anointed, fr. mashakh to anoint. Cf. Messias.

messuage.etymology: Cf. OF. mesuage, masnage, LL. messuagium, mansionaticum, fr. L. mansio, -onis, a staying, remaining, dwelling, fr. manere, mansum, to stay, remain, E. mansion, manse.

mestizo.etymology: Sp. mestizo; akin to OF. mestis, F. métis; all fr. (assumed) LL. mixtitius, fr. L. mixtus mixed, p. p. of miscere to mix. See Mix, and cf. Mestee, MÉtif, MÉtis, Mustee.

metal.etymology: F. métal, L. metallum metal, mine, Gr. Mettle, Medal.

metallic.etymology: L. metallicus, fr. metallum: cf. F. métallique. See Metal.

metalloid.etymology: L. metallum metal + -oid: cf. F. métalloïde.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

metallurgy.etymology: F. métallurgie, fr. L. metallum metal, Gr. Metal, and Work.

roots.meaning: A combining form meaning part, portion; as, blastomere, epimere.

metaphor.etymology: F. métaphore, L. metaphora, fr. Gr. meta` beyond, over + fe`rein to bring, bear.

metaphysics.etymology: Gr. métaphysique. See Physics. The term was first used by the followers of Aristotle as a name for that part of his writings which came after, or followed, the part which treated of physics.

metathesis.etymology: L., fr. Gr. meta`thesis, fr. metatithe`nai to place differently, to transpose; meta` beyond, over + tithe`nai to place, set. See Thesis.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

metheglin.etymology: W. meddyglyn; medd mead + llyn liquor, juice. See Mead a drink.

method.etymology: F. méthode, L. methodus, fr. Gr. meqodos method, investigation following after; meta` after + "odo`s way.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

methylene.etymology: F. méthylène, from Gr. wood spirit.

meticulous.etymology: L. meticulosus, fr. metus fear: cf. F. méticuleux.

metis.etymology: F.; akin to Sp. mestizo. See Mestizo.

metonymy.etymology: L. metonymia, Gr. métonymie. See Name.

metre.etymology: OE. metre, F. mètre, L. metrum, fr. Gr. ma to measure. See Mete to measure.

metric.etymology: L. metricus, Gr. métrique. See Meter rhythm.

metrify.etymology: L. metrum meter + -fy: cf. F. métrifier.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

metropolis.etymology: L. metropolis, Gr. Mother, and Police.

mettle.etymology: E. metal, used in a tropical sense in allusion to the temper of the metal of a sword blade. See Metal.

mew.etymology: AS. m, akin to D. meeuw, G. möwe, OHG. m, Icel. mar.

mewl.etymology: Cf. F. miauler to mew, E. mew to cry as a cat. Cf. Miaul.

mews.etymology: Prop. pl. of mew. See Mew a cage.

mezzanine.etymology: F. mezzanine, It. mezzanino, fr. mezzano middle, fr. mezzo middle, half. See Mezzo.

mezzo.etymology: It., from L. medius middle, half. See Mid, a.

miaul.etymology: Cf. F. miauler, of imitative origin, and E. mew. Cf. Mewl.

mica.etymology: L. mica crumb, grain, particle; cf. F. mica.

michaelmas.etymology: Michael + mass religious service; OE. Mighelmesse.

mickle.etymology: OE. mikel, muchel, mochel, mukel, AS. micel, mycel; akin to OS. mikil, OHG. mihil, mihhil, Icel. mikill, mykill, Goth. mikils, L. magnus, Gr. mahat. sq. root103. Cf. Much, Muckle, Magnitude.

micturition.etymology: L. micturire to desire to make water, v. desid. fr. mingere, mictum, to make water.

mid.etymology: AS. midd; akin to OS. middi, D. mid (in comp.), OHG. mitti, Icel. mi, Goth. midjis, L. medius, Gr. madhya. Amid, Middle, Midst, Mean, Mediate, Meridian, Mizzen, Moiety.

midas.etymology: So called from L. Midas, a man fabled to have had ass's ears.

midday.etymology: AS. middæg. See Mid, a., and Day.

midden.etymology: Cf. Dan. mögdynge, E. muck, and dung.

middle.etymology: OE. middel, AS. middel; akin to D. middel, OHG. muttil, G. mittel. Mid, a.

midriff.etymology: AS. midhrif; midd mid, middle + hrif bowels, womb; akin to OFries. midref midriff, rif, ref, belly, OHG. href body, and to L. corpus body. See Corpse.

midst.etymology: From middest, in the middest, for older in middes, where -s is adverbial (orig. forming a genitive), or still older a midde, a midden, on midden. See Mid, and cf. Amidst.

midwife.etymology: OE. midwif, fr. AS. mid with (akin to Gr. Meta-, and Wife.

mien.etymology: F. mine; perh. from sane source as mener to lead; cf. E. demean, menace, mine, n.

miff.etymology: Cf. Prov. G. muff sullenness, sulkiness, muffen to be silky, muffïg sullen, pouting.

might.etymology: AS. meaht, miht, from the root of magan to be able, E. may; akin to D. magt, OS. maht, G. macht, Icel. mattr, Goth. mahts. May, v.

mighty.etymology: AS. meahtig, mihtig; akin to G. mächtig, Goth. mahteigs. See Might, n.

mignonette.etymology: F. mignonnette, dim. of mignon darling. See 2d Minion.

migrant.etymology: L. migrans, p. pr. of migrare. See Migrate.

migrate.etymology: L. migratus, p. p. of migrare to migrate, transfer.

milch.etymology: OE. milche; akin to G. melk, Icel. milkr, mj, and to E. milk. See Milk.

mildew.etymology: AS. meledeáw; akin to OHG. militou, G. mehlthau, mehltau; prob. orig. meaning, honeydew; cf. Goth. milip honey. See Mellifluous, and Dew.

mile.etymology: AS. mil, fr. L. millia, milia; pl. of mille a thousand, i. e., milia passuum a thousand paces. Cf. Mill the tenth of a cent, Million.

milfoil.etymology: F. mille-feuille, L. millefolium; mille thousand + folium leaf. See Foil a leaf.

milieu.etymology: F., fr. mi middle (L. medius) + lieu place. See Demi-, Lieu.

roots.meaning: A prefix, signifying half.

militant.etymology: L. militans, -antis, p. pr. of militare to be soldier: cf. F. militant. See Militate.

military.etymology: L. militaris, militarius, from miles, militis, soldier: cf. F. militaire.

militate.etymology: L. militare, militatum, to be a soldier, fr. miles, militis, soldier.

militia.etymology: L., military service, soldiery, fr. miles, militis, soldier: cf. F. milice.

milk.etymology: AS. meoluc, meoloc, meolc, milc; akin to OFries. meloc, D. melk, G. milch, OHG. miluh, Icel. mj, Sw. mjölk, Dan. melk, Goth. miluks, G. melken to milk, OHG. melchan, Lith. milszti, L. mulgere, Gr. Milch, Emulsion, Milt soft roe of fishes.

mill.etymology: L. mille a thousand. Cf. Mile.

millenary.etymology: L. millenarius, fr. milleni a thousand each, fr. mille a thousand: cf. F. millénaire. See Mile.

millennium.etymology: From Late Latin mīllennium , from Latin mīllennis ( “ 1000 - year ” ) + -ium ( forming abstract nouns ) .

millerite.etymology: From W. H. Miller, of Cambridge, Eng.

millet.etymology: F., dim. of mil, L. milium; akin to Gr. mil.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting a thousandth part of; as, millimeter, milligram, milliampère.

milliard.etymology: F., from mille, mil, thousand, L. mille.

milligram.etymology: F. milligramme; milli- milli- + gramme. See 3d Gram.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting a thousandth part of; as, millimeter, milligram, milliampère.
A prefix denoting a thousandth part of; as, millimeter, milligram, milliampère.

milliliter.etymology: F. millilitre; milli- milli- + litre. See Liter.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting a thousandth part of; as, millimeter, milligram, milliampère.
A prefix denoting a thousandth part of; as, millimeter, milligram, milliampère.

millilitre.etymology: F. millilitre; milli- milli- + litre. See Liter.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting a thousandth part of; as, millimeter, milligram, milliampère.
A prefix denoting a thousandth part of; as, millimeter, milligram, milliampère.

millimeter.etymology: F. millimètre; milli- milli- + mètre. See 3d Meter.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting a thousandth part of; as, millimeter, milligram, milliampère.
A prefix denoting a thousandth part of; as, millimeter, milligram, milliampère.

millimetre.etymology: F. millimètre; milli- milli- + mètre. See 3d Meter.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting a thousandth part of; as, millimeter, milligram, milliampère.
A prefix denoting a thousandth part of; as, millimeter, milligram, milliampère.

milliner.etymology: From Milaner an inhabitant of Milan, in Italy; hence, a man from Milan who imported women's finery.

million.etymology: F., from LL. millio, fr. L. mille a thousand. See Mile.

milord.etymology: F. (also It., Sp., Russ.), fr. E. my lord.

milt.etymology: AS. milte; akin to D. milt, G. milz, OHG. milzi, Icel. milti, Dan. milt, Sw. mjälte, and prob. to E. malt, melt. sq. root108. See Malt the grain.

mime.etymology: L. mimus, Gr. mime. Cf. Mimosa.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.

mimic.etymology: L. mimicus, Gr. mimique. See Mime.

minaret.etymology: Sp. minarete, Ar. manarat lamp, lantern, lighthouse, turret, fr. nar to shine.

minatory.etymology: L. minatorius, fr. minari to threaten. See Menace.

mince.etymology: AS. minsian to grow less, dwindle, fr. min small; akin to G. minder less, Goth. minniza less, mins less, adv., L. minor, adj. (cf. Minor); or more likely fr. F. mincer to mince, prob. from (assumed) LL. minutiare. Minish.

mind.etymology: AS. mynd, gemynd; akin to OHG. minna memory, love, G. minne love, Dan. minde mind, memory, remembrance, consent, vote, Sw. minne memory, Icel. minni, Goth. gamunds, L. mens, mentis, mind, Gr. manas mind, man to think. Comment, Man, Mean, v., 3d Mental, Mignonette, Minion, Mnemonic, Money.

mineral.etymology: F. minéral, LL. minerale, fr. minera mine. See Mine, v. i.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

minge.etymology: AS. myngian; akin to E. mind.

mingle.etymology: From OE. mengen, AS. mengan; akin to D. & G. mengen, Icel. menga, also to E. among, and possibly to mix. Cf. Among, Mongrel.

miniate.etymology: L. miniatus, p. p. of miniare. See Minium.

miniature.etymology: It. miniatura, fr. L. miniare. See Miniate, v.,Minium.

minibus.etymology: L. minor less + -bus, as in omnibus.

minim.etymology: F. minime, L. minimus the least, smallest, a superl. of minor: cf. It. minima a note in music. See Minor, and cf. Minimum.

minion.etymology: F. mignon, fr. OHG. minni love, G. minne; akin to E. mind. See Mind, and cf. Mignonette.

minister.etymology: OE. ministre, F. ministre, fr. L. minister, orig. a double comparative from the root of minor less, and hence meaning, an inferior, a servant. See 1st Minor, and cf. Master, Minstrel.

ministerial.etymology: L. ministerialis: cf. F. ministériel. See Minister, and cf. Minstrel.

ministrant.etymology: L. ministrans, -antis, of ministrare to minister.

ministry.etymology: L. ministerium. See Minister, n., and cf. Mystery a trade.

minium.etymology: L. minium, an Iberian word, the Romans getting all their cinnabar from Spain; cf. Basque armineá.

minnow.etymology: OE. menow, cf. AS. myne; also OE. menuse, OF. menuise small fish; akin to E. minish, minute.

minor.etymology: L., a comparative with no positive; akin to AS. min small, G. minder less, OHG. minniro, a., min, adv., Icel. minni, a., minnr, adv., Goth. minniza, a., mins, adv., Ir. & Gael. min small, tender, L. minuere to lessen, Gr. mi to damage. Cf. Minish, Minister, Minus, Minute.

minority.etymology: Cf. F. minorité. See Minor, a. & n.

minotaur.etymology: L. Minotaurus, Gr. Mi`nos, the husband of Pasiphaë + tay^ros a bull, the Minotaur being the offspring of Pasiphaë and a bull: cf. F. minotaure.

minster.etymology: AS. mynster, fr. L. monasterium. See Monastery.

minstrel.etymology: OE. minstrel, menestral, OF. menestrel, fr. LL. ministerialis servant, workman (cf. ministrellus harpist), fr. L. ministerium service. See Ministry, and cf. Ministerial.

mint.etymology: AS. mynet money, coin, fr. L. moneta the mint, coined money, fr. Moneta, a surname of Juno, in whose at Rome money was coined; akin to monere to warn, admonish, AS. manian, and to E. mind. See Mind, and cf. Money, Monition.

minuend.etymology: L. minuendus to be diminished, fr. minuere to lessen, diminish. See Minish.

minuet.etymology: F., fr. menu small, L. minutus small. So called on account of the short steps of the dance. See 4th Minute.

minus.etymology: L. See Minor, and cf. Mis- pref. from the French.

roots.meaning: A prefix used adjectively and adverbially in the sense of amiss, wrong, ill, wrongly, unsuitably; as, misdeed, mislead, mischief, miscreant.

minuscule.etymology: L. minusculus rather small, fr. minus less: cf. F. minuscule.

minute.etymology: LL. minuta a small portion, small coin, fr. L. minutus small: cf. F. minute. See 4th Minute.

minutia.etymology: L., fr. minutus small, minute. See 4th Minute.

minx.etymology: Prob. of Low German origin; cf. LG. minsk wench, jade, hussy, D. mensch; prop. the same word as D. & G. mensch man, human being, OHG. mennisco, AS. mennisc, fr. man. See Man.

miracle.etymology: F., fr. L. miraculum, fr. mirari to wonder. See Marvel, and cf. Mirror.

mirage.etymology: F., fr. mirer to look at carefully, to aim, se mirer to look at one's self in a glass, to reflect, to be reflected, LL. mirare to look at. See Mirror.

mire.etymology: OE. mire, myre; akin to Icel. m swamp, Sw. myra marshy ground, and perh. to E. moss.

mirror.etymology: OE. mirour, F. miroir, OF. also mireor, fr. (assumed) LL. miratorium, fr. mirare to look at, L. mirari to wonder. See Marvel, and cf. Miracle, Mirador.

mirth.etymology: OE. mirthe, murthe, merthe, AS. myredh, myrgedh, merhedh, mirhedh. See Merry.

miscegenation.etymology: L. miscere to mix + the root of genus race.

miscellaneous.etymology: Borrowed from Latin miscellāneus , from miscellus ( “ mixed ” ) , from misceō ( “ mix ” ) .

miscellany.etymology: L. miscellanea, neut. pl. of. miscellaneus: cf. F. miscellanée, pl. miscellanées. See Miscellaneous.

mischief.etymology: OE. meschef bad result, OF. meschief; pref. mes- (L. minus less) + chief end, head, F. chef chief. See Minus, and Chief.

roots.meaning: See Meso-.

miscible.etymology: Cf. F. miscible, fr. L. miscere to mix.

miscount.etymology: Cf. OF. mesconter, F. mécompter. Cf. Miscompute.

miscreant.etymology: OF. mescreant, F. mécréant; pref. mes- (L. minus less) + p. pr. fr. L. credere to believe. See Creed.

roots.meaning: See Meso-.

miser.etymology: L. miser wretched, miserable; cf. Gr. misero wretched, avaricious.

miserable.etymology: F. misérable, L. miserabilis, fr. miserari to lament, pity, fr. miser wretched. See Miser.

misery.etymology: OE. miserie, L. miseria, fr. miser wretched: cf. F. misère, OF. also, miserie.

misfeasance.etymology: OF. pref. mes- wrong (L. minus less) + faisance doing, fr. faire to do, L. facere. Cf. Malfeasance.

roots.meaning: See Meso-.

mishmash.etymology: Cf. G. mish-mash, fr. mischen to mix.

mishna.etymology: NHeb. mishnah, i. e., repetition, doubling, explanation (of the divine law), fr. Heb. shanah to change, to repeat.

mislead.etymology: AS. misl. See Mis-, and Lead to conduct.

roots.meaning: A prefix used adjectively and adverbially in the sense of amiss, wrong, ill, wrongly, unsuitably; as, misdeed, mislead, mischief, miscreant.

misnomer.etymology: OF. pref. mes- amiss, wrong (L. minus less) + F. nommer to name, L. nominare, fr. nomen name. See Name.

roots.meaning: See Meso-.

missal.etymology: LL. missale, liber missalis, from missa mass: cf. F. missel. See 1st Mass.

missile.etymology: L. missils, fr. mittere, missum, to cause to go, to send, to throw; cf. Lith. mesti to throw: cf. F. missile. Cf. Admit, Dismiss, Mass the religious service, Message, Mission.

mission.etymology: L. missio, fr. mittere, missum, to send: cf. F. mission. See Missile.

missionary.etymology: Cf. F. missionnaire. See Mission, n.

mist.etymology: AS. mist; akin to D. & Sw. mist, Icel. mistr, G. mist dung, Goth. maíhstus, AS. migan to make water, Icel. miga, Lith. migla mist, Russ. mgla, L. mingere, meiere, to make water, gr. mih to make water, n., a mist m*gha cloud. *102. Cf. Misle, Mizzle, Mixen.

mistake.etymology: Pref. mis- + take: cf. Icel. mistaka.

roots.meaning: A prefix used adjectively and adverbially in the sense of amiss, wrong, ill, wrongly, unsuitably; as, misdeed, mislead, mischief, miscreant.

mistime.etymology: AS. mistimain to turn out ill.

mistletoe.etymology: AS. misteltan; mistel mistletoe + tan twig. AS. mistel is akin of D., G., Dan. & Sw. mistel, OHG. mistil, Icel. mistilteinn; and AS. tan to D. teen, OHG. zein, Icel. teinn, Goth. tains. Cf. Missel.

mistress.etymology: OE. maistress, OF. maistresse, F. maîtresse, LL. magistrissa, for L. magistra, fem. of magister. See Master, Mister, and cf. Miss a young woman.

misty.etymology: AS. mistig. See Mist. In some senses misty has been confused with mystic.

misuse.etymology: F. mésuser. See Mis-, prefix from French, and Use.

roots.meaning: A prefix used adjectively and adverbially in the sense of amiss, wrong, ill, wrongly, unsuitably; as, misdeed, mislead, mischief, miscreant.

mite.etymology: AS. mite mite (in sense 1); akin to LG. mite, D. mijt, G. miete, OHG. miza; cf. Goth. maitan to cut.

mitigate.etymology: L. mitigatus, p.p. of mitigare to soften, mitigate; mitis mild, soft + the root of agere to do, drive.

mitigation.etymology: OE. mitigacioun, F. mitigation, fr. L. mitigatio.

mitten.etymology: OE. mitaine, meteyn, F. mitaine, perh. of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. miotog, Gael. miotag, Ir. & Gael. mutan a muff, a thick glove. Cf. Mitt.

mix.etymology: AS. miscan; akin to OHG. misken, G. mischen, Russ. mieshate, W. mysgu, Gael. measg, L. miscere, mixtum, Gr. miçra mixed. The English word has been influenced by L. miscere, mixtum (cf. Mixture), and even the AS. miscan may have been borrowed fr. L. miscere. Cf. Admix, Mash to bruise, Meddle.

mixture.etymology: L. mixtura, fr. miscere, mixtum, to mix: cf. F. mixture. See Mix.

mizzen.etymology: It. mezzana, fr. mezzano middle, fr. mezzo middle, half: cf. F. misaine foresail. See Mezzo.

moan.etymology: AS. m to moan, also, to mean; but in the latter sense perh. a different word. Cf. Mean to intend.

moat.etymology: OF. mote hill, dike, bank, F. motte clod, turf: cf. Sp. & Pg. mota bank or mound of earth, It. motta clod, LL. mota, motta, a hill on which a fort is built, an eminence, a dike, Prov. G. mott bog earth heaped up; or perh. F. motte, and OF. mote, are from a LL. p.p. of L. movere to move (see Move). The name of moat, properly meaning, bank or mound, was transferred to the ditch adjoining: cf. F. dike and ditch.

mobcap.etymology: D. mop-muts; OD. mop a woman's coif + D. muts cap.

mobile.etymology: L. mobilis, for movibilis, fr. movere to move: cf. F. mobile. See Move.

mock.etymology: F. moquer, of uncertain origin; cf. OD. mocken to mumble, G. mucken, OSw. mucka.

mode.etymology: L. modus a measure, due or proper measure, bound, manner, form; akin to E. mete: cf. F. mode. See Mete, and cf. Commodious, Mood in grammar, Modus.

model.etymology: F. modèle, It. modello, fr. (assumed) L. modellus, fr. modulus a small measure, dim. of modus. See Mode, and cf. Module.

moderate.etymology: L. moderatus, p.p. of moderate, moderati, to moderate, regulate, control, fr. modus measure. See Mode.

modern.etymology: F. moderne, L. modernus; akin to modo just now, orig. abl. of modus measure; hence, by measure, just now. See Mode.

modest.etymology: F. modeste, L. modestus, fr. modus measure. See Mode.

modesty.etymology: L. modestia: cf. F. modestie. See Modest.

modicum.etymology: L., fr. modicus moderate, fr. modus. See Mode.

modification.etymology: L. modificatio a measuring: cf. F. modification. See Modify.

modify.etymology: F. modifier, L. modificare, modificari; modus limit + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Mode, and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

modillion.etymology: F. modillon, It. modiglione. Cf. Module, n.

modiste.etymology: F. See Mode, and cf. Modist.

modulate.etymology: L. modulatus, p.p. of modulari to measure, to modulate, fr. modulus a small measure, meter, melody, dim. of modus. See Mode.

module.etymology: F., fr. L. modulus a small measure, dim. of modus. See Mode, and cf. Model, Modulus, Mold a matrix.

modulus.etymology: L., a small measure. See Module, n.

mohair.etymology: F. moire, perh. from Ar. mukhayyar a kind of coarse camelot or haircloth; but prob. fr. L. marmoreus of marble, resembling marble. Cf. Moire, Marble.

mohammedan.etymology: From Mohammed, fr. Ar. muhámmad praiseworthy, highly praised.

moiety.etymology: F. moitié, L. medietas, fr. medius middle, half. See Mid, a., and cf. Mediate, Mediety.

moil.etymology: OE. moillen to wet, OF. moillier, muillier, F. mouller, fr. (assumed) LL. molliare, fr. L. mollis soft. See Mollify.

moist.etymology: OE. moiste, OF. moiste, F. moite, fr. L. muccidus, for mucidus, moldy, musty. Cf. Mucus, Mucid.

molasses.etymology: F. mélasse, cf. Sp. melaza, Pg. melaço, fr. L. mellaceus honeylike, honey-sweet, mel, mellis, honey. See Mellifluous, and cf. Melasses.

molder.etymology: From Mold fine soft earth: cf. Prov. G. multern.

moldy.etymology: From Mold the growth of fungi.

mole.etymology: AS. mal; akin to OHG. meil, Goth. mail Cf. Mail a spot.

molecule.etymology: Dim. fr. L. moles a mass: cf. F. molécule. See 3d Mole.

molest.etymology: F. molester, L. molestare, fr. molestus troublesome, fr. moles a heavy mass, load, burden. See 3d Mole.

moline.etymology: L. molina mill, fr. molere to grind. See Mill.

moll.etymology: G., fr. L. mollis soft, tender, elegiac. Cf. Molle.

mollify.etymology: F. mollifier, L. mollificare; mollis soft + - ficare (in comp.) to make. See Enmollient, Moil, v. t., and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

mollusk.etymology: F. mollusque, L. mollusca a kind of soft nut with a thin shell, fr. molluscus soft, mollis soft. See Mollify.

molt.etymology: OE. mouten, L. mutare. See Mew to molt, and cf. Mute, v. t.

molybdenum.etymology: NL.: cf. F. molybdène. See Molybdena.

moment.etymology: F. moment, L. momentum, for movimentum movement, motion, moment, fr. movere to move. See Move, and cf. Momentum, Movement.

momot.etymology: Momot and motmot, the native American name.

mona.etymology: CF. Sp. & Pg. mona, fem. of mono a monkey, ape.

monarch.etymology: F. monarque, L. monarcha, fr. Gr. Archi-.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying chief, arch; as, architect, archiepiscopal. In Biol. and Anat. it usually means primitive, original, ancestral; as, archipterygium, the primitive fin or wing.

monarchy.etymology: F. monarchie, L. monarchia, Gr. Monarch.

roots.meaning: Same as Mono-.

monday.etymology: OE. moneday, monenday, AS. monandæg, i.e., day of the moon, day sacred to the moon; akin to D. maandag, G. montag, OHG. manatag, Icel. manadagr, Dan. mandag, Sw. måndag. See Moon, and Day.

monetary.etymology: L. monetarius belonging to a mint. See Money.

money.etymology: OE. moneie, OF. moneie, F. monnaie, fr. L. moneta. See Mint place where coin is made, Mind, and cf. Moidore, Monetary.

moneyer.etymology: From Money; cf. OF. monoier, F. monnoayeur, L. monetarius a master of the mint. Cf. Monetary.

monger.etymology: AS. mangere, fr. mangian to trade; akin to Icel. manga to trade, mangari a trader, OHG. mangari, mengari; cf. L. mango a dealer in slaves.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

mongrel.etymology: Prob. shortened fr. mongrel, and akin to AS. mengan to mix, and E. mingle. See Mingle.

monition.etymology: F., fr. L. monitio, from monere to warn, bring to mind; akin to E. mind. See Mind, and cf. Admonish, Money, Monster.

monitor.etymology: L., fr. monere. See Monition, and cf. Mentor.

monk.etymology: AS. munuc, munec, munc, L. monachus, Gr. Monachism.

monkey.etymology: Cf. OIt. monicchio, It. monnino, dim. of monna an ape, also dame, mistress, contr. fr. madonna. See Madonna.

monogram.etymology: L. monogramma; Gr. monogramme. See Graphic.

monovalent.etymology: Mono- + L. valens, p. pr. See Valence.
